name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,357

clue.text: Old Queen’s dog and old Queen presented in cinematic effects?

indicators.note: To be presented in something is to appear inside it, so the letters named go within the ones that follow.

blocks.note: CGI is computer-generated imagery, the effects added to a film after it is shot
o = old
r = Regina, the Latin the Queen signs with

explanation.surface: A royal pet and a long-dead monarch both turning up in a film's special effects.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth II kept the breed from girlhood until her death, which is why naming her is enough to name the dog. 'Queen' does duty twice in one clue, once in the definition and once as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth II owned corgis for seventy years and was rarely photographed without one, so the breed is identified by its most famous owner.

clue.text: Humourless Lord supporting company

indicators.note: What supports something holds it up from below, so in a down entry the supporting piece goes underneath.

blocks.note: co. is the written short form of company
Ld is the written abbreviation for Lord

explanation.surface: A joyless peer propping up a business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' is a whole instruction in a down clue: the thing doing the supporting is at the bottom, so the firm sits on top of the peer. Cold for humourless is the sense in 'a cold reception'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold manner has no warmth or laughter in it, the sense in 'a cold stare', which is what calling someone humourless describes.

clue.text: Telephone equipment brought about ultimate in communication

indicators.note: To bring a thing about is to bring it round, and a word brought round another closes on either side of it.
The ultimate is the last, so only the closing letter of the word after it is taken.

blocks.note: a rig is equipment, the gear set up for a particular job
the closing letter of COMMUNICATION

explanation.surface: Phone gear fetched round for the last word in getting in touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telephone' is the verb — to ring somebody — rather than the object the rest of the sentence is fetching. RIG is worth stocking as a word for equipment: it covers an oil platform, a lorry and a sailing ship's gear alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring someone is to telephone them, so definition and answer are the same verb for placing a call.

clue.text: Reported money received by crooked person in office

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by mouth, so the words are to be heard rather than read.

blocks.note: the money you receive is your income, and said aloud it lands on these five letters
bent = crooked, of a nail or of a policeman

explanation.surface: Word going round that a dishonest official has been taking payments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Received by' invites you to post one word inside another, and the two halves simply stand side by side. The homophone is a single letter's worth of difference, which is what makes it hard to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: The incumbent is whoever currently holds a post, so the definition is the standard phrase for exactly that office-holder.

clue.text: Job overseas, working in the mailroom?

blocks.note: the appointment an army or a firm sends you abroad to take up
what you are doing when you send the letters off

explanation.surface: An overseas appointment that turns out to involve sorting the mail.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a letter moves: the same word covers a career step abroad and an afternoon franking envelopes. The question mark is the setter owning up to the drop between the two.
explanation.definitionFit: A posting is the job you are sent away to fill; and to post is the British verb for mailing a letter, which is the mailroom's whole trade.

clue.text: Schoolchildren turned up with beer

indicators.note: A thing turned is swung round to face the other way, so the word beside it is read backwards.

blocks.note: the two letters of UP written backwards
pils is pilsner, the pale lager

explanation.surface: Schoolchildren arriving with a crate of lager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as one phrase — they arrived — and splits into an instruction and the two letters it acts on. Pils is short for pilsner, the pale lager first brewed in Bohemia.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils are the children taught at a school, the British word where an American would say students.

clue.text: Marine creature losing tail in ocean

indicators.note: The tail of a word is the letter at its end, and losing it takes that letter off.

blocks.note: a seal is a marine creature, here with its last letter taken off

explanation.surface: An animal that has lost its tail somewhere out in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Losing a tail is a real hazard for an animal, which is what keeps the surface innocent; here it happens to the word instead. The creature wanted is the obvious one, and the clue keeps three-quarters of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea and ocean are the same expanse of salt water, one word standing in for the other in ordinary use.

clue.text: Asian country mainly supplies staff for ship

indicators.note: Mainly means in the main — the greater part of a thing rather than all of it — so the word it marks gives up its last letter.

blocks.note: India is a country of southern Asia
to man a post is to supply staff for it, and MANS surrenders its last letter

explanation.surface: An Asian country providing most of the crew for a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: An Indiaman was a merchant ship licensed to the East India Company, built for the long haul round the Cape to Bombay and Canton. Crewing a vessel is exactly the business such a ship was in, which is why the surface holds together.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indiaman was a large armed merchantman of the East India trade, so the definition names the class and leaves the solver to supply the trade route.

clue.text: Leave various dates alongside unknown date

indicators.note: Various things differ from one another, and letters made to differ from the order given are letters to rearrange.

blocks.note: to leave is to go
the five letters of DATES resettled
y is the algebraist's unknown quantity

explanation.surface: Walking out on a string of assorted dates for the sake of one nobody can name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dates' is raw material the first time and the definition the second, where it is the verb a courting couple would use. Y for an unknown comes from algebra, alongside x and z.
explanation.definitionFit: To go steady is to date one person regularly and exclusively, so the definition is the plain verb for the same arrangement.

clue.text: Roughly cleans soft camera accessory

indicators.note: A job done roughly comes out untidy, and untidy letters are letters knocked out of their proper order.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
p = piano, the musical direction to play softly

explanation.surface: Giving something soft that belongs with a camera a quick careless wipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft' is the musician's p rather than anything about the cloth, and 'roughly' is the shuffle rather than the manner of the wiping. A lens cap is the cover that keeps grit off the front element.
explanation.definitionFit: A lens cap is the small cover clipped over a camera lens, exactly the sort of extra that 'accessory' covers.

clue.text: A name of the French mountains

blocks.note: the article taken at face value
n = name
des is French for 'of the'

explanation.surface: A French word for some mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: The mountains the surface points at are the Alps or the Pyrenees; the range wanted is on the other side of the Atlantic. Des for 'of the' is one of the few scraps of French an English crossword assumes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are the chain running the whole western length of South America, so the plural definition names the range by its kind.

clue.text: Better with famous boxer to speak about the writer

indicators.note: To be about something is to be round it.

blocks.note: Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight champion
the setter pointing at himself inside his own clue
to orate is to speak, formally and at length

explanation.surface: A well-known fighter making a speech about the person who wrote this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is the verb, to improve, and not the comparative adjective the sentence offers. Ali is the crossword's standard boxer, and 'the writer' is always the setter pointing at himself.
explanation.definitionFit: To ameliorate a situation is to make it better, so the definition is the everyday verb for the same act of improvement.

clue.text: Honour is excellent, securing new deference

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast, and a word holding another keeps it shut inside.

blocks.note: the Order of the British Empire, the award announced in the New Year honours list
the verb taken at face value
ace = excellent
n = new

explanation.surface: A gong is a fine thing, winning its holder fresh respect.
explanation.walkthrough: OBE is the Order of the British Empire, a medal handed out twice a year by the palace, and it appears whenever a crossword mentions an honour. Obeisance is the bow itself as much as the respect behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeisance is deference made visible — the bow or gesture of submission, and by extension the respect it stands for.

clue.text: Commotion? Mob becoming half-hearted is desirable

indicators.note: A word's heart is the letters at its centre, and going half-hearted gives up half of what is beating there.

blocks.note: ado = fuss, as in much ado about nothing
a mob is a rabble, and RABBLE has a doubled B at its centre that surrenders one

explanation.surface: A rioting crowd going off the boil, which would suit everybody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-hearted' is exact rather than vague: the word it works on carries two letters at its centre and hands over one. The question mark after the first word marks it off as a separate piece rather than part of the mob.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adorable is something you long to have about you, and that longing is what makes a thing desirable.

clue.text: Bird-handler in old France botched clipping bird’s tail

indicators.note: A botched job has come out wrong all through, and letters that have come out wrong are letters in the wrong order.
Clipping a tail cuts off what comes last, and the tail meant is the final letter of the word BIRD, so a D is what goes.

blocks.note: OLD with its final D cut off, two letters of raw material
six more letters of raw material

explanation.surface: A man who handles birds, back in old France, making a mess of docking a tail.
explanation.walkthrough: The two birds do different jobs: the first names the trade, the second is there only to give up its final letter. Falconry was the sport of the medieval French nobility, which is what the surface is leaning on.
explanation.definitionFit: A falconer is the person who trains and flies hawks, so the definition names the trade by what it handles.

clue.text: Draughtsman’s daughter, less refined

blocks.note: d = daughter, as on a family tree
raw is what unrefined material is called, so less refined is rawer

explanation.surface: A draughtsman's daughter with rougher manners than her father.
explanation.walkthrough: A drawer is the thing in a desk far more often than it is a person who draws, which is why the definition has to spell out the trade. Refining is what happens to raw sugar and raw oil, so less of it is rawer.
explanation.definitionFit: A draughtsman draws for a living and a drawer is one who draws, the agent noun standing in for the name of the trade.

clue.text: Conflict blocking Communist honour

indicators.note: What blocks a thing stands in its way, and a word standing in another's way sits in the middle of it.

blocks.note: a red is a Communist, after the colour of the flag
a war is a conflict

explanation.surface: A war standing in the way of a Communist's decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: Red for Communist goes back to the flag and the Red Army and is the crossword's usual shorthand. The two halves of the wordplay are the same sort of word, which hides which one is doing the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: An honour and a reward are both handed over in recognition of what somebody has done, the one word covering the medal and the other the prize.

clue.text: Lingerie item more expensive? That’s an error

blocks.note: a slip is the light underskirt worn beneath a dress
a price that is up has gone higher

explanation.surface: An underskirt that has gone up in price.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the leap from 'more expensive' to the two letters of a price rise. A slip is the plain underskirt, and it is the one piece of lingerie a crossword ever asks for.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip-up is a mistake — the same slip as in 'a slip of the tongue', turned into a noun for any small blunder.

clue.text: Performer, it’s clear, getting excited about it

indicators.note: Somebody worked up is thoroughly stirred, and stirred letters come out in a new order.
To be about a thing is to be round it, so the stirred letters close on either side of the word that follows.

blocks.note: the eight letters of IT'S CLEAR resettled, the apostrophe ignored
the pronoun taken at face value

explanation.surface: A performer, obviously, who is working himself up about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's clear' reads as the setter's aside and is eight letters of raw material; the little 'it' at the end is the one word that keeps its own spelling. A recitalist is the musician who gives a solo recital.
explanation.definitionFit: A recitalist is someone who gives recitals — a soloist on a platform — so 'Performer' names the class the word sits in.

clue.text: Peaceful type runs away from Channel port

indicators.note: What is taken away from a word leaves it, so the letter named goes out of the name that follows.

blocks.note: the Kent harbour town facing Calais across the Strait
r = runs, from the cricket scorebook

explanation.surface: A gentle soul fleeing from a port on the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: R for runs comes straight off a cricket scorecard, the source of a good many of the crossword's single letters. The peaceable sense is the opposite number of the hawk, a pairing borrowed from politics rather than from ornithology.
explanation.definitionFit: In politics a dove is the one arguing for peace against the hawk who wants the fight, so 'peaceful type' means the person rather than the bird.

clue.text: Line ignored by fast runners?

indicators.note: What is ignored is left out, so the letter named is dropped from the word that follows.

blocks.note: fleet means swift, and the word gives up its L
l = line

explanation.surface: A boundary that the quickest runners take no notice of.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is an apology: these are not runners, they are what a runner runs on. 'Fleet' for fast survives chiefly in 'fleet of foot', which is the phrase the answer has been cut out of.
explanation.definitionFit: Feet are what carry a runner along, so the definition names them by the job they do rather than by what they are — hence the question mark.

clue.text: Excessive activity for one point, on reflection

indicators.note: A reflection shows a thing back to front, so the letters assembled are read the other way round.

blocks.note: e.g. is for example, so 'for one' is the same two letters
the point of a pen is its nib

explanation.surface: Far too much effort spent on a single point, once you think it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' reads as a change of mind and means back to front. 'Point' is the pen's nib here, not a mark in a game or a bearing on a compass.
explanation.definitionFit: A binge is a bout of unrestrained drinking, eating or spending — activity carried well past what anyone would call sensible.

clue.text: Slippery customer ends in the police cell

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, and the three words that follow end in the three letters wanted.

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the three words in turn

explanation.surface: A shifty character finishing up in a police cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ends in the police cell' reads as a whole sentence about where a crook finishes up, and is three separate final letters. The definition is a stock phrase for a shifty person, borrowed from a creature nobody can keep hold of.
explanation.definitionFit: A slippery customer is someone impossible to pin down, and the eel is the animal that phrase takes its slipperiness from.

clue.text: European taking in hot camera feature?

indicators.note: To take a thing is to take hold of it, so the word doing the taking closes round what comes next.

blocks.note: a Pole is a European
the word itself, taken at face value
h = hot, the letter on a tap

explanation.surface: A European soaking up the hot weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking in' looks like one instruction and is not: only 'taking' does the enclosing, and the 'in' is two of the letters enclosed. A pinhole camera has no lens at all — light through one tiny aperture makes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinhole is the tiny aperture a lensless camera forms its image through, so 'camera feature' points at a hole rather than at any fitting.

clue.text: Restriction on hearing to merit endless fuss

indicators.note: Endless means without its end, so the last letter of the word before it comes off.

blocks.note: to merit is to earn, and EARN gives up its final letter
a flap is a fuss, as in 'don't get in a flap'

explanation.surface: A curb on what can be heard, deserving no end of fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' is a court hearing in the surface and the plain business of the ear in the definition. The definition describes what the thing does to you rather than what it is, which is why it sounds like a regulation.
explanation.definitionFit: An earflap is the hinged piece of a cap that folds down over the ear, muffling whatever you might otherwise have heard.

clue.text: English respond, dismissing American? Straight up

indicators.note: To dismiss somebody is to send them away, so the letter named is sent out of the word holding it.

blocks.note: e = English
to respond is to react
a = American, the letter dropped from the verb

explanation.surface: The English reacting by sending an American packing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the odd job the American is doing: he is one letter to be removed, not a person being snubbed. 'Straight up' is upright, the way a post stands, and not the assurance that something is true.
explanation.definitionFit: Something erect stands straight upright, so the definition is the plain physical sense rather than the slang for honestly.
